hints: Focus on the word self. Ask yourself for each option, did this molecule come from your own body cells or from an invader?
Remember that self antigens are normal cell surface markers on your own cells that the immune system learns to tolerate, while anything viral or pathogen-made is non-self.
walkthrough:
**Understand what self means**

Think of self as anything made by your own body. Non-self is anything foreign that your immune system should attack.

So we just need to sort each molecule into self or non-self.

**Check where each molecule comes from**

A viral capsid protein, a viral envelope phospholipid and a pathogen toxin are all made by or part of a pathogen. They are foreign to you.

A macrophage is one of your own white blood cells, so its surface glycoprotein is made by you.

**Pick the self antigen**

Your immune system must recognise your own macrophage markers as self so it does not attack them. That makes the macrophage glycoprotein the only possible self antigen.

options.A: This is a non-self antigen because it is part of a virus, so the immune system will recognise it as foreign and attack it.
options.B: This is a non-self antigen because it is part of a viral envelope, not a molecule made by your own cells.
options.C: This is a non-self antigen because it is released by a pathogen, so it will trigger an immune response, not tolerance.
options.D: This is correct because a macrophage is your own cell, so its surface glycoprotein is a self marker that your immune system learns to tolerate.
